SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 jobs as it remakes itself as an "AI first" company

meldungen.titel: Consulting Deep Dive, part 12: operations and supply chain, the practice that builds future COOs
meldungen.text:
If strategy work asks what a company should do, operations work asks how it actually gets done: how a plant runs, how parts reach the line, how much a company pays its suppliers and how many people it needs to serve a customer. It is the least glamorous corner of consulting and, measured by the number of projects and consultants, one of the largest. Every major firm has an operations practice, but they differ markedly in weight and style.

McKinsey runs the most structured version. Its Operations Practice spans manufacturing and supply chain, procurement, service operations and capital projects (the firm calls the latter Capital Excellence), and it offers a dedicated early-career route, the Operations Excellence Program, which it describes as a competence centre where more than 600 consultants have started their careers. More experienced specialists can join its Advanced Operations Group. On its careers pages, McKinsey stresses that operations consultants work on the same client teams as generalists but bring deeper functional expertise, which makes the practice a natural home for engineers and people with an industrial background.

Bain sells operations largely through its performance improvement work and its COO agenda, tying cost and supply chain programmes closely to profit targets, which also makes it a frequent adviser to private equity owners trying to lift margins in portfolio companies. Kearney, by contrast, is known above all for procurement, supply chain and manufacturing work, and its operations partners are a regular source of hires for rivals.

The projects are concrete: cutting procurement spend through supplier renegotiation, redesigning a production network after tariffs, reducing inventory, setting up a lean programme in a plant or restructuring a service centre. Consultants spend more time on site than in the boardroom, often in factories and warehouses, and the results are measurable in euros, which partly explains why the practice weathers downturns better than pure strategy work.

The exits follow from that. Large manufacturers and industrial groups hire former consultants into procurement, supply chain, logistics and operational excellence roles, and career guides describe this route as the most network-driven of all consulting exits: placements tend to come through former clients rather than headhunters. One typical industry listing accepts three years of consulting in place of five years of functional experience. After project leader level, typical moves are head of procurement, director of operations or transformation lead, and from there the path runs towards chief operating officer or chief supply chain officer. Private equity firms, which increasingly employ in-house operating partners, are another natural destination.

A good example of how fluid the field is: Benoit Gougeon began in supply chain and finance at L'Oréal, joined Kearney in Paris in 2006, led its operations practice there as partner and has since moved to Bain. A former Bain consultant, Michael Dumais, became chief transformation officer at Raytheon Technologies.

As for schools, operations practices recruit through the same campus channels as the generalist track, so a MiM from HEC, HSG or WHU opens the door equally; what tips the balance is quantitative depth and a credible interest in industry, often shown through an internship in manufacturing or logistics.

meldungen.titel: SAP weighs cutting at least 10,000 jobs as it remakes itself as an "AI first" company
meldungen.text:
Europe's most valuable software company is preparing another round of deep cuts. SAP is weighing the elimination of at least 10,000 positions, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the plans. That would be close to a tenth of its workforce of roughly 110,000. Every department has reportedly been told to identify posts that could go, with product development, product support and sales in particular focus. SAP did not deny the report and said only that it continuously reviews its organisation to keep it aligned with strategy and customer needs.

The plan is not final, and the number could change after talks with employee representatives. SAP has traditionally announced large restructurings in late January alongside its annual results, so a formal decision is likely then. Investors welcomed the prospect of a leaner company and pushed the shares up by almost 2 percent.

The logic is chief executive Christian Klein's push to make SAP "AI first". The company has bought four AI and data firms this year, among them the US data specialist Reltio, the lakehouse platform Dremio, the Belgian skills platform TechWolf and the Freiburg lab Prior Labs, into which it plans to invest more than a billion euros over four years. Since the summer it has restricted new hiring mainly to AI roles. Internally, SAP says its Joule assistant has made finance, HR and procurement noticeably more productive, and that developers now produce far more code than at the start of the year.

The cuts do not stem from weakness. In the third quarter, SAP's quarterly revenue passed 10 billion euros for the first time, with cloud revenue growing fastest. That is precisely what makes the move telling: a profitable, growing company is reshaping its workforce because it expects software to do work that people did before. Separately, SAP confirmed on Friday morning an IT incident affecting development systems, reportedly hosted on GitHub, though it did not confirm a Spiegel report describing it as a hacker attack.

SAP has done this before. Its 2024 restructuring ultimately covered about 10,000 roles, relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining, and cost around 3 billion euros; because the company hired in growth areas at the same time, headcount ended up roughly flat. In Germany, a works agreement offers some protection: affected staff are to be offered other roles and retraining. The union IG Metall is unimpressed, arguing that the agreement mainly sets the level of severance, "a price tag for dismissals", rather than ruling out compulsory redundancies.

Whether AI is really replacing jobs on this scale is disputed. An analysis by Oxford Economics found that AI accounted for only a small share of announced job cuts in the United States last year, and that productivity has not risen as it should if machines were taking over large amounts of work. Some firms, critics suggest, cite AI because it sounds better to investors than weak demand or earlier over-hiring. SAP is in good company either way: Salesforce and Workday have made similar cuts in the name of AI.

meldungen.titel: After a bad night, strong coffee before breakfast pushes blood sugar up, a study from Bath suggests
meldungen.text:
Reaching for a strong black coffee after a broken night is one of the most common morning rituals there is. A study from the University of Bath, published in the British Journal of Nutrition, suggests that the timing matters: drunk on an empty stomach, that coffee makes the body handle the sugar from breakfast noticeably worse.

The researchers, led by Harry Smith, tested 29 young, healthy volunteers under three conditions. After a normal night, participants drank a sugary solution designed to mimic breakfast. After a disrupted night, during which they were woken every hour, they drank the same solution. In the third condition, also after a broken night, they first drank strong black coffee and took the sugar drink half an hour later. Blood samples tracked glucose and insulin.

The surprising finding was that one bad night on its own made little difference to blood sugar. The coffee did. When participants had it before their "breakfast", their blood sugar response rose by about half, according to several reports on the study.

The study has clear limits. The sample was small, the participants were young and healthy, and the effect was measured after a single night and a single drink, not over weeks. Some commentators therefore warn against reading too much into it. Nobody is suggesting that coffee itself is unhealthy; the advice is simply about order.

The practical upshot is easy to follow: if you need caffeine after a short night, eat first and drink the coffee with or after breakfast rather than on an empty stomach. The finding matters most for people whose sleep is regularly broken, such as shift workers, because for them the bad night and the coffee are a daily combination rather than an exception.

meldungen.titel: A federal judge blocks the Trump administration's review of ABC's broadcast licences, calling retaliation against satire unconstitutional
meldungen.text:
A federal court in Washington has handed Disney and its network ABC an important win in their fight with the Trump administration. On Wednesday, US District Judge Loren AliKhan issued a preliminary injunction blocking the government from pursuing its challenge to the licences of ABC's local television stations, NPR reported. She ruled that a president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional, and she rejected the administration's request to dismiss the lawsuit altogether.

The dispute goes back to earlier this year, when the Federal Communications Commission under its chairman Brendan Carr ordered eight ABC-owned stations to file applications to renew their broadcast licences years ahead of schedule. Licences normally run for eight years and are rarely revoked, so the early review was widely read as pressure on a network whose satire and commentary the president has repeatedly attacked. Disney and ABC sued the FCC and Carr in August, arguing that the review was punishment for protected speech.

The government's case rested on procedure. Its lawyers argued at an October hearing that the district court had no jurisdiction because such disputes belong before a different venue, that the FCC had not yet reached any decision, and that ABC had not shown irreparable harm. ABC's counsel, Beth Wilkinson, countered that the harm lay in the threat itself: "The irreparable injury is the chill." AliKhan's ruling leaned heavily on the president's own public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, and on comments by Carr.

The order is preliminary, so the case itself continues, and the administration can appeal. It is nonetheless one of the clearest judicial limits so far on the use of regulatory power against the media. It also comes at a moment when the political balance in Washington is shifting: after their midterm victories, Democrats will control both chambers of Congress, and oversight of the FCC is likely to intensify.

meldungen.titel: EU: the Commission floats a 50 billion euro equity fund for "sovereign" technology, but the gap it targets lies elsewhere
meldungen.text:
The decision. The European Commission, through its executive vice-president for tech sovereignty Henna Virkkunen, has set out plans for a Quantum Act, reported this week by the Austrian start-up outlet brutkasten. Its centrepiece is a Sovereign Tech Equity Fund of 50 billion euros, meant to provide equity and similar financing for technologies critical to Europe's technological sovereignty and economic security. The money would not go to quantum alone but also to AI and other areas covered by the Commission's Tech Sovereignty Package. The act itself rests on three pillars: research excellence, industrial application, and secure systems and supply chains.

The case made. The Commission argues that Europe lost the race in AI for lack of ambition and money, and must not repeat the mistake in quantum. "Europe must now pick up the pace," Virkkunen said. The fund is meant to turn strong research into industrial capacity. The strongest objection is that the Commission has not said where the money would come from; France and Germany have urged that the act focus on procurement, funding and governance rather than ambitions alone.

The numbers. In quantum, the problem is not public money: the EU spent more public funds on quantum last year than the United States, according to figures compiled by Reuters. Private money is another story; US investors put roughly six times as much private capital into the field as European ones. Across all venture capital, the United States invested roughly four times as much in early- and growth-stage rounds as the EU in 2025, according to Dealroom data cited in Intereconomics, and the gap widens sharply at later stages. The OECD adds the decisive detail: early-stage funding in Europe is broadly comparable, and companies fall behind only when they try to scale.

Reality check. The data support the Commission's diagnosis that Europe has a financing gap, and that it is concentrated in late-stage, large-ticket rounds. A big equity fund is aimed at the right stage. What the data do not support is the implied claim that public money is the missing ingredient: in quantum, public spending is already high, and analysts at the ECB and in Intereconomics point instead to Europe's narrow investor base, with pension funds supplying a far smaller share of venture money than in the United States, and to fragmented capital markets. Funding is a further unknown. Trade press reporting on the draft act earlier this month found no overall spending figure in it, and independent coverage of the 50 billion euro fund remains thin, so its size, sources and timetable are unconfirmed. Whether the EU should hold equity stakes in companies at all is a value judgement that data cannot settle.

Evidence rating: Partly grounded. The funding gap at the scale-up stage is well documented, but the proposal leaves unexplained how the money would be raised and why public equity would fix a problem that the evidence locates mainly in private capital.
